name: Epidermal growth factor (EGF)

angle.text: EGF is a growth-factor protein sold in skincare serums to rejuvenate skin and reduce wrinkles. The biology is well established, while evidence for the cosmetic use is one tiny serum trial with no published results.

summary: A growth-factor protein sold in skincare serums; real biology, one tiny serum trial with no published results.
note: EGF signaling is studied in cancer biology; cosmetic safety is untested.
currentQuick:
Epidermal growth factor is a natural protein that tells cells to grow and divide. Its discoverers won a Nobel Prize, and it appears in some cosmetic serums.
A recombinant form is used for diabetic foot ulcers. For skin appearance, only one small registered serum trial was found, with no published results.
How it works: EGF binds its receptor EGFR on cells, triggering signaling that drives proliferation and survival.
Risks and caveats: Safety of medical EGF is described as poorly studied, and EGF signaling is a research focus in cancers. No study found has tested cosmetic EGF for cancer risk.
deepLead:
Epidermal growth factor (EGF) is a small protein of 53 amino acids that stimulates cell growth, differentiation and survival by binding the EGF receptor (EGFR) on cell surfaces . It was the second growth factor to be identified; Stanley Cohen found it while working with Rita Levi-Montalcini, and the two shared the 1986 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine .
In cosmetics, recombinant or synthetic EGF appears as an ingredient in some serums, where marketing describes it as supporting skin renewal and repair. In looksmaxxing and skincare discussion it is grouped with other growth-factor and peptide skincare ingredients.
Medically, a recombinant human EGF product (Heberprot-P) is used for diabetic foot ulcers, with evidence of improved healing described as tentative and safety described as poorly studied . One small registered trial has examined an EGF facial serum for skin aging, with no published results found .

name: CJC/IPA Protocol

angle.text: CJC/IPA pairs CJC-1295 with ipamorelin and is popular on forums for muscle, leanness and recovery. The combination is untested in trials and neither part is approved; forum claims also mention water retention changing the face and eyes.

summary: The common GH-releasing peptide pairing; popular on forums, untested as a combination, neither part approved.
note: Unapproved research peptides; CJC-1295 research stopped after a trial death.
currentQuick:
CJC/IPA combines a long-acting GHRH analogue with a selective GH secretagogue to raise growth hormone. Forum users take it for body composition and appearance.
No trial has tested the pair, and neither compound is an approved drug.
How it works: CJC-1295 mimics GHRH; ipamorelin activates the ghrelin receptor; both prompt GH release.
Risks and caveats: CJC-1295 research was stopped after a participant died (attributed to unrelated coronary disease by the physician). Users report water retention. Both are WADA-prohibited and sold as research peptides.
deepLead:
CJC/IPA refers to the combined use of CJC-1295, a long-acting analogue of growth hormone-releasing hormone (GHRH), and ipamorelin, a selective ghrelin-receptor (growth hormone secretagogue) agonist, both aimed at raising growth hormone (GH) release . Neither is an approved drug.
On looksmax.org, the pairing is discussed by users who buy it as research peptides, with threads about side effects such as facial water retention and about whether it affects growth plates in teenagers .
No published trial has tested the combination for appearance outcomes. The two compounds were studied separately: CJC-1295 reached phase II trials before research was stopped, and ipamorelin failed a phase II trial for postoperative ileus .

name: Tesa/IPA Protocol

angle.text: Tesa/IPA stacks tesamorelin with ipamorelin and is used in peptide circles for fat loss and body composition. Tesamorelin has trial data for visceral fat in a specific patient group, while the combination has no trials.

summary: A tesamorelin plus ipamorelin injectable peptide stack for fat loss; each part has some history, the combination has no trials.
note: Tesamorelin is Rx-only; ipamorelin is unapproved and WADA-prohibited.
currentQuick:
Tesa/IPA means using the prescription GHRH analogue tesamorelin together with the unapproved peptide ipamorelin, mainly for fat loss.
Tesamorelin is approved for HIV-associated lipodystrophy. Ipamorelin was abandoned in clinical development. No trial has tested the pair.
How it works: Tesamorelin mimics growth-hormone-releasing hormone; ipamorelin activates the ghrelin receptor. Both raise growth hormone and hence IGF-1.
Risks and caveats: Tesamorelin labelling-type effects include injection-site reactions, edema, joint pain and glucose intolerance. Ipamorelin is unapproved and appears on the WADA prohibited list.
deepLead:
The Tesa/IPA protocol is a term used in peptide and body-composition circles for combining two injectable growth-hormone-axis peptides, tesamorelin and ipamorelin. The two are different substances: tesamorelin is a synthetic analogue of growth-hormone-releasing hormone (GHRH), while ipamorelin is a pentapeptide that acts on the ghrelin (growth hormone secretagogue) receptor. 
Tesamorelin is a prescription drug sold by Theratechnologies as Egrifta, initially approved in 2010 for HIV-associated lipodystrophy.  Ipamorelin was developed by Novo Nordisk, later tested by Helsinn Therapeutics for postoperative ileus, and abandoned for lack of efficacy; it is not an approved drug and is commonly sold as a research peptide. 
Proponents pair the two on the theory that they release growth hormone through different receptors and could be used for fat loss. No published trial has tested the combination in humans, and the sources reviewed describe neither agent as an approved cosmetic treatment.

name: GT20029

angle.text: GT20029 is an investigational topical AR-degrading PROTAC for male pattern hair loss and acne, discussed as a possible alternative to finasteride without systemic exposure. It has a published Phase 2 trial and is not approved.

summary: An experimental topical AR-degrading PROTAC for male pattern hair loss, with a published Phase 2 trial and no approval.
note: Investigational; only early-phase trials, mainly in Chinese men.
currentQuick:
GT20029 is an investigational gel or solution from Kintor Pharmaceutical meant to remove androgen receptors from scalp skin.
A 180-man Phase 2 trial in China has been published; it is not approved anywhere.
How it works: It is a PROTAC: it marks the androgen receptor for destruction by the proteasome, aiming to act locally.
Risks and caveats: Phase 1 and 2 safety data exist but detailed long-term data do not. It is unavailable as a regulated product.
deepLead:
GT20029 is an investigational topical androgen receptor (AR) degrader developed by Kintor Pharmaceutical of China for androgenetic alopecia and acne. It is a PROTAC (proteolysis-targeting chimera), a type of molecule that tags a target protein for destruction by the cell's proteasome rather than merely blocking it. 
A 2025 review of topical PROTACs names GT20029 and AH-001 as AR degraders in clinical trials for androgenetic alopecia, with the aim of localised degradation and lower systemic exposure.  Phase 1 safety trials were completed, and a Phase 2 trial in 180 Chinese men with Hamilton-Norwood III vertex to V alopecia has been published. 
It is not approved anywhere. Forum users have followed its trial news with interest as a possible non-systemic alternative to finasteride-type drugs.

name: Liposomal IGF-1

angle.text: Liposomal IGF-1 is discussed for scalp application because IGF-1 promotes follicle proliferation and the growth phase in lab work. The use is plausible on paper, and the evidence for it is preclinical.

summary: IGF-1 in liposomes for the scalp; the biology is plausible on paper but evidence is preclinical.
note: No human hair-loss trial found.
currentQuick:
Liposomal IGF-1 is a topical idea: deliver the growth factor IGF-1 to hair follicles inside fat-like carriers.
IGF-1 is naturally produced in the follicle, but studies of the topical product in people were not found.
How it works: IGF-1 acts on dermal papilla cells, promoting growth-phase signalling through PI3K/Akt and MAPK/ERK. [1]
Risks and caveats: Safety of topical IGF-1 on the scalp has not been established in published trials; it is an unapproved product for hair.
deepLead:
Liposomal IGF-1 refers to insulin-like growth factor 1 packaged in liposomes for topical application to the scalp. IGF-1 is a growth factor made mainly by dermal papilla cells in hair-bearing skin; a 2025 review reports that it stimulates follicle proliferation and vascularization and promotes the growth (anagen) phase through PI3K/Akt and MAPK/ERK signalling. 
Community interest rests largely on animal and laboratory work. No clinical trial of a liposomal topical IGF-1 for hair loss appears among the sources reviewed.

name: Hedgehog pathway agonist

angle.text: Hedgehog pathway agonists were explored as topical hair-growth drugs because the pathway moves follicles from rest to growth. The class was discontinued, with development reportedly ended over animal toxicity.

summary: A discontinued class of topical hair-growth compounds that activated Hedgehog signaling; development reportedly ended over animal toxicity.
note: Not available as a product; no human efficacy data found.
currentQuick:
Hedgehog pathway agonists were explored as hair-growth agents because the pathway helps follicles enter the growth phase.
Wikipedia says the effort failed on animal toxicity. No human results were found.
How it works: They activate Smoothened/GLI signaling, the opposite of anticancer Smoothened inhibitors such as vismodegib.
Risks and caveats: The reported reason for stopping was toxicity in animal models. Pathway activation in general is a concern in tissue-growth contexts, and no product is available.
deepLead:
Hedgehog pathway agonists are small molecules that switch on the Hedgehog signaling pathway, which guides embryonic development and regulates adult stem cells. The pathway is reported to be required for hair follicles to move from the resting phase into the growth phase, which is why agonists were explored as hair-growth drugs. 
One program is associated in community discussion with Curis and Procter & Gamble. According to Wikipedia, the hair-growth effort failed because of toxicities found in animal models.  No marketed product exists, and the sources reviewed describe no human efficacy data.

name: Adenosine (topical hair)

angle.text: Topical adenosine is a cosmetic active in hair-growth products, used by people hoping to thicken thinning hair. Laboratory work reports activity on dermal papilla cells, while human evidence for this use is not established here.

summary: A cosmetic hair-growth active with plausible lab data on dermal papilla cells; human evidence not established here.
note: Evidence mostly in vitro.
currentQuick:
Topical adenosine is an ingredient in some hair-growth cosmetics, supported mainly by cell and follicle-culture studies.
A 2024 paper suggests an anti-androgen-receptor effect in addition to growth-factor stimulation.
How it works: It raises FGF-2 and FGF-7 in dermal papilla cells and prolongs the growth phase; it may also dampen AR signalling. [1][2]
Risks and caveats: Safety data were not covered by the sources reviewed; it is sold as a cosmetic ingredient.
deepLead:
Adenosine is a naturally occurring nucleoside used as a cosmetic active in hair-growth products. Laboratory work reports that it acts on dermal papilla cells, the follicle's signalling center. 
A 2012 study in cultured mouse whisker follicles found that adenosine stimulated dermal papilla growth and lengthened the anagen (growth) phase by raising cysteine levels through fibroblast growth factors 2 and 7.  A 2024 paper examined an adenosine complex's effects on gene expression in dermal papilla cells and identified the androgen receptor pathway as a candidate target, distinct from minoxidil's mechanism.

name: Procyanidin B2

angle.text: Procyanidin B2 is an apple polyphenol used in hair-growth tonics and discussed as a natural option for thinning hair. The evidence includes lab, mouse and small human studies, mostly using whole extracts rather than the compound alone.

summary: An apple polyphenol with early lab, mouse and small human data for hair growth, mostly using whole extracts.
note: Evidence is for extracts, not isolated B2.
currentQuick:
Procyanidin B2 is a polyphenol found in apples, promoted as a hair-growth ingredient.
Research includes cell studies, mouse studies and one randomized trial of an Annurca apple formulation.
How it works: Proposed actions include protecting hair epithelial cells from TGF-beta-induced apoptosis and boosting keratin expression. [2]
Risks and caveats: Dietary procyanidins are common in food; safety of concentrated supplements was not assessed in the sources reviewed.
deepLead:
Procyanidin B2 is a B-type dimer of the procyanidin subgroup of proanthocyanidins, polyphenols built mainly from catechin and epicatechin units. Apples are a notable dietary source of proanthocyanidins. 
Apple-derived procyanidins, and procyanidin B2 in particular, have been studied for hair growth. A PubMed search listing shows research on procyanidin oligomers in hair epithelial cells, apple-extract studies in mice, and a 2018 randomized clinical trial of an Annurca apple formulation; the abstracts describe the Annurca extracts as rich in procyanidin B2.  Evidence is early and based largely on extracts rather than the pure compound.

name: Garlic gel

angle.text: Garlic gel is a folk preparation used for patchy hair loss from alopecia areata, mostly discussed in non-prescription regrowth contexts. Evidence for that use is one terminated children's trial.

summary: A folk garlic preparation for patchy hair loss with one terminated children's trial behind it and a record of skin burns when applied raw.
note: Raw garlic on skin has caused burns.
currentQuick:
Garlic gel is a home or alternative remedy applied to the scalp for alopecia areata, an autoimmune cause of patchy hair loss.
The only registered trial found was a small phase 3 study in children that began in 2016 and was terminated after eight participants, with no results posted.
How it works: Proponents of garlic remedies generally say that it irritates or stimulates the scalp and encourages regrowth. No mechanism has been established in the sources available for this entry.
Risks and caveats: Raw garlic applied to skin has been reported to cause burns, and references advise caution especially in young children [2]. It is not an approved treatment for alopecia areata.
deepLead:
Garlic gel is a topical preparation made from garlic (Allium sativum) that has been used as a folk or alternative treatment for alopecia areata, an autoimmune condition that causes patchy hair loss. It is discussed mainly in the context of non-prescription approaches to hair regrowth rather than in appearance-optimisation forums specifically.
Only one registered clinical trial of a garlic preparation for alopecia areata appears in the registry record for this entry: a phase 3 study of a topical garlic concentrate in children that began in January 2016, enrolled eight participants and was terminated . The registry entry lists no results, so no efficacy conclusion can be drawn from it.
Garlic applied raw to the skin has been reported to cause burns, and general references on garlic advise caution with topical use, particularly in young children .

name: Avobenzone

chain: Fewer wrinkles and dark spots over time
angle.text: Avobenzone is the main organic UVA filter in US sunscreens and is used by people who want to slow photoageing and keep skin looking younger. UVA protection for photoageing is its studied purpose; it needs stabilisers in sunlight.

summary: The main organic UVA filter in US sunscreens: widely used for photoageing protection, unstable in sunlight without stabilisers, absorbed into the bloodstream.
note: FDA says more safety data are needed; it is photounstable.
currentQuick:
Avobenzone is a chemical sunscreen filter that absorbs UVA light, the part of sunlight linked to photoageing. It is found in many sunscreens and SPF moisturisers.
It breaks down in sunlight unless paired with stabilisers like octocrylene. FDA-sponsored trials found it is absorbed into the blood after application.
How it works: Its conjugated structure absorbs UVA photons and releases the energy as heat, reducing UV reaching skin cells [1].
Risks and caveats: Regulators have asked for more safety data on systemic absorption; the studies measured blood levels, not harm. Allergy and environmental concerns have been reported, and Palau banned it in 2020 [2]. It is OTC; limits are 3% in the US and 5% in the EU.
deepLead:
Avobenzone (butyl methoxydibenzoylmethane, trade name Parsol 1789) is an oil-soluble organic compound used as a UVA filter in chemical sunscreens and in moisturisers and cosmetics that carry an SPF claim . It absorbs ultraviolet light across much of the UVA range, with an absorption peak near 357 nm .
It is notable for being the main UVA-absorbing organic filter permitted in the United States, at up to 3%, while the European Union permits up to 5% . It is photounstable, losing absorbance under sunlight unless formulated with stabilisers such as octocrylene .
In 2019 and 2020, randomised trials sponsored by the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) found that avobenzone and other sunscreen ingredients enter the bloodstream after topical use at concentrations above the 0.5 ng/mL threshold the agency had set for further safety study . The authors and regulators stated that this finding does not by itself show that the ingredients are unsafe.

name: Octinoxate

chain: Fewer sunspots and wrinkles over time
angle.text: Octinoxate is a common UVB filter in sunscreens and SPF lip balms, used by skincare-minded people to keep skin looking younger and avoid sunburn and uneven tone. Its UVB absorption is well characterised; its appearance benefit comes through sun protection generally rather than trials of this filter alone.

summary: The common organic UVB filter in sunscreens and lip balms, absorbed into the blood and flagged for endocrine activity in lab work, yet judged safe at 10% by the EU's SCCS in 2025.
note: Restricted in Hawaii and Palau on reef grounds.
currentQuick:
Octinoxate is a chemical sunscreen filter that absorbs UVB, the burning part of sunlight. It is common in sunscreens, SPF lip balms and cosmetics.
It has been debated because lab studies reported hormone-like activity and trials show it enters the bloodstream. The EU's SCCS concluded in 2025 that it is safe up to 10%.
How it works: It absorbs UVB radiation (about 290-320 nm) and dissipates the energy as heat. Sunlight can convert it to a form that absorbs less, so it is usually stabilised with other filters [1][2].
Risks and caveats: Reported concerns are endocrine activity in cell and animal studies, systemic absorption, and coral reef effects; human clinical harm has not been shown in the studies listed. Hawaii and Palau restrict it. Allowed levels: 7.5% US, 10% EU.
deepLead:
Octinoxate (octyl methoxycinnamate, ethylhexyl methoxycinnamate, OMC) is an organic UVB filter used in sunscreens, lip balms and cosmetics with SPF claims . It absorbs UVB with a peak near 310 nm and is typically combined with other filters .
It has drawn regulatory and scientific attention for endocrine activity seen in laboratory and animal studies, for systemic absorption in humans, and for its use being restricted in places such as Hawaii and Palau on environmental grounds . The European Commission's Scientific Committee on Consumer Safety (SCCS) published an opinion in June 2025 concluding it is safe at up to 10% in cosmetics, according to both encyclopedia sources .

name: Oxybenzone

chain: Fewer sunspots and wrinkles over time
angle.text: Oxybenzone is a broad-spectrum sunscreen filter used in sunscreens and lip products so skin stays smoother and more even-toned in the sun. The anti-aging case rests on sunscreen-class evidence for UV protection, not on studies of oxybenzone's own effect on appearance.

summary: A broad-spectrum sunscreen filter found in most people's urine, linked to reef-damage findings and banned in places like Hawaii, yet still legal under US federal rules.
note: Banned in Hawaii and several other jurisdictions; EU limits apply.
currentQuick:
Oxybenzone is an organic sunscreen filter that absorbs both UVB and part of UVA light. It was long among the most common sunscreen ingredients, though its use in US sunscreens has declined.
It is controversial because it is absorbed into the body, detected in most people tested in a US survey, and linked in lab studies to coral damage.
How it works: Its aromatic ketone structure absorbs UV photons between about 270 and 350 nm and releases the energy as heat [1][2].
Risks and caveats: Reported issues include skin allergy, systemic absorption, endocrine activity in lab assays and coral toxicity findings. Hawaii, the US Virgin Islands, Palau, Aruba and others restrict it; the FDA lists it as lacking sufficient safety data but it remains legal.
deepLead:
Oxybenzone (benzophenone-3, BP-3) is an organic UV filter that absorbs UVB and short-wave UVA, used in sunscreens, lip products, hair sprays, nail polish and as a stabiliser in plastics . It was first synthesised in 1906 by Bernhard König and Stanisław Kostanecki and later developed as a sunscreen ingredient from the 1950s, according to Grokipedia .
It is one of the most debated sunscreen ingredients. Biomonitoring found it in about 97% of US urine samples tested in 2003-2004 , clinical trials show it is absorbed through the skin , and laboratory work links it to coral damage . Several jurisdictions, including Hawaii, have banned sales of sunscreens containing it . In the United States the FDA classes it as not yet shown to be generally recognised as safe and effective because of insufficient data, while it remains legal .

name: Octisalate

angle.text: Octisalate is a mild UVB filter added to sunscreens to lift SPF and keep filters like avobenzone stable, so daily sunscreen can protect skin from photoaging. It is also an emollient that adds water resistance. Evidence is for sunscreen formulas as a class, not octisalate alone.

summary: A weak UVB filter used mostly to lift SPF and steady other filters; absorbed through skin in small amounts and under European endocrine testing requirements.
note: ECHA required endocrine-related fish testing in 2020.
currentQuick:
Octisalate is a salicylate-based sunscreen ingredient that absorbs a little UVB light. Its main job is to raise SPF and help keep other filters like avobenzone from breaking down.
Because it is a minor filter, it has far less research than headline ingredients, mostly absorption and allergy studies.
How it works: It absorbs UVB and also acts as an emollient that adds water resistance to formulas [1].
Risks and caveats: A 2020 trial found it enters the bloodstream; Wikipedia says under 1% penetrates skin and sensitisation potential is minor. European regulators required endocrine-related testing; it is classed as highly toxic to aquatic life in REACH registrations [1].
deepLead:
Octisalate (octyl salicylate, 2-ethylhexyl salicylate) is an ester of salicylic acid used in sunscreens and cosmetics as a weak UVB absorber, usually added to boost SPF and to help stabilise other filters such as avobenzone and oxybenzone . It is also an emollient that adds water resistance .
It is one of the six active ingredients assessed in 2020 JAMA trial of sunscreen absorption, which found that all were absorbed into the bloodstream . Regulators in Europe have required additional endocrine-related testing, which a company contested unsuccessfully in court .

name: Homosalate

angle.text: Homosalate is a common UVB filter in sunscreens, used for daily protection that helps keep skin looking even-toned and younger. Its appearance benefit is inferred from sunscreen-class evidence on UV damage rather than studies of homosalate specifically.

summary: A common UVB sunscreen filter whose possible hormone-like activity has led to EU concentration limits and animal-testing demands; human harm has not been shown.
note: EU concentration limit; endocrine questions under review.
currentQuick:
Homosalate is a chemical sunscreen ingredient that absorbs UVB light and is used to build SPF. It is reported in roughly 45% of US sunscreens.
European regulators have examined it for hormone-like effects seen in lab assays. Summaries disagree on how firm the concern is, and no human harm has been demonstrated in the studies listed.
How it works: Its salicylate group absorbs UVB and its bulky ring keeps it from washing out in water [2].
Risks and caveats: It is absorbed into blood after sunscreen use per a 2020 trial. Lab studies report anti-androgenic and estrogenic activity; the EU has set a concentration limit and required further testing, and it has been measured in coastal waters and coral tissue.
deepLead:
Homosalate (3,3,5-trimethylcyclohexyl salicylate) is a salicylate ester used as an organic UVB filter in sunscreens and SPF cosmetics . It absorbs UVB at roughly 295-315 nm and is reported to be found in about 45% of US sunscreens .
It is under scrutiny in Europe for possible endocrine activity. Wikipedia reports a June 2021 SCCS opinion finding no sufficient evidence that pure homosalate is an endocrine disruptor in humans , whereas Grokipedia states the committee considered it acceptable only up to 0.5% in certain cosmetics because of unresolved endocrine concerns . The two summaries differ and the primary opinions were not consulted for this article.

name: Ensulizole

angle.text: Ensulizole is used in light, non-greasy facial lotions and daily moisturisers, so people can wear sun protection under makeup every day and slow sun-driven skin aging. Evidence is sunscreen-class, not specific to appearance outcomes of this filter.

summary: A water-soluble UVB sunscreen filter for light facial lotions; evidence is sunscreen-class, not appearance-specific.
note: Mainly UVB; needs other filters for UVA coverage.
currentQuick:
Ensulizole is an organic sunscreen filter that absorbs mostly UVB light. Because it dissolves in water, it appears in light lotions and daily facial moisturisers with SPF.
It is an approved US over-the-counter sunscreen active. Published research on ensulizole alone is thin; most of what exists covers sunscreen ingredients generally.
How it works: It absorbs UVB radiation in the skin-surface layer of a product. It offers little UVA protection, so it is usually combined with filters such as avobenzone, zinc oxide or bemotrizinol.
Risks and caveats: Sunscreen filters as a group can cause allergic or photoallergic reactions in some people, and labels advise stopping use if rash or irritation occurs. Environmental studies have detected PBSA in water and examined effects on fish and mussels.
deepLead:
Ensulizole, also known as phenylbenzimidazole sulfonic acid (PBSA) and 2-phenylbenzimidazole-5-sulfonic acid, is a water-soluble organic ultraviolet (UV) filter used in sunscreens and daily facial moisturisers. It is primarily a UVB absorber with minimal UVA coverage, so it is generally combined with other filters when broad-spectrum protection is intended.
Its water solubility, achieved by using the compound as a neutralised salt, lets formulators add it to the water phase of lotions and gels, which proponents of light, non-greasy sunscreens cite as its main attraction. In the United States it is a monograph (over-the-counter) sunscreen active, and its name has appeared on US sunscreen labels since 1999.
Published human research on ensulizole specifically is sparse. Most literature concerns sunscreens as a class, photoallergy surveys, in vitro efficacy comparisons and environmental detection in water; none of it tests ensulizole as a looksmaxxing or cosmetic-appearance intervention.

name: Ecamsule

angle.text: Ecamsule (Mexoryl SX) is a photostable UVA filter prized in European and Asian sunscreens by users wanting protection against the UVA rays linked to wrinkling and pigmentation. Its use in sunscreens is established; appearance outcomes are inferred from UVA protection in general.

summary: L'Oreal's photostable UVA filter, Mexoryl SX; established in sunscreens abroad, US-approved only via NDA products.
note: Systemic absorption above the FDA's 0.5 ng/mL threshold was measured in a 2019 trial.
currentQuick:
Ecamsule (Mexoryl SX) is a UVA-absorbing sunscreen ingredient developed by L'Oreal in the 1980s. It is valued for photostability and is usually paired with other filters.
It has been sold in Europe and Canada since the 1990s; in the US it is approved only in sunscreens registered through a New Drug Application.
How it works: It absorbs UVA light and dissipates the energy as heat, remaining chemically stable under sunlight.
Risks and caveats: A 2019 JAMA trial found sunscreen actives including ecamsule were absorbed into plasma above the FDA's screening threshold; the authors did not conclude this meant harm. Other sources describe low systemic effects and no photomutagenicity in vitro.
deepLead:
Ecamsule, sold under the trade name Mexoryl SX and known by the INCI name terephthalylidene dicamphor sulfonic acid, is a photostable organic UVA filter developed and patented by L'Oreal in 1982. It absorbs ultraviolet light between roughly 290 and 400 nm, with a peak near 345 nm, and is typically combined with other filters (such as avobenzone and octocrylene) because it does not cover the whole UV range on its own.
Sunscreens containing it have been sold in Europe, Canada and elsewhere since 1993. In the United States the FDA approved it in 2006 only within sunscreens registered under a New Drug Application, rather than as a general over-the-counter monograph ingredient.
Published human studies on ecamsule-containing sunscreens report protection against UV-induced skin changes, and a 2019 trial measured absorption into the bloodstream under maximal-use conditions. No trial has examined it as a standalone appearance treatment.

name: Bemotrizinol

angle.text: Bemotrizinol (Tinosorb S) is a favourite among skincare enthusiasts for broad-spectrum, photostable sunscreens, often sought from EU, Australian and Asian products to protect skin from aging UV. Evidence is from sunscreen testing and long regional use rather than appearance trials.

summary: A photostable broad-spectrum UV filter long used in EU, Australian and Asian sunscreens and reportedly newly cleared in the US.
note: US approval is recent; registry entries do not report trial outcomes.
currentQuick:
Bemotrizinol is an oil-soluble sunscreen filter that covers both UVB and UVA and is very photostable. It has been used in EU sunscreens since 2000.
It was absent from US sunscreens for years; Wikipedia reports FDA approval in June 2026.
How it works: It absorbs UV light across about 280-400 nm and converts it to heat, and it helps stabilise filters like avobenzone.
Risks and caveats: Registered trials of a 6% sunscreen examined absorption, phototoxicity, photoallergy and irritation. Lab studies found no estrogenic activity, and aquatic toxicity studies exist.
deepLead:
Bemotrizinol (INCI: bis-ethylhexyloxyphenol methoxyphenyl triazine, BEMT; trade names Tinosorb S, Escalol S, Parsol Shield) is an oil-soluble organic UV filter that absorbs both UVB and UVA, with absorption peaks around 310 and 340-345 nm. It is noted for photostability and for helping stabilise less stable filters such as avobenzone.
It has been approved in the European Union since 2000 and in Australia, and is widely used in sunscreens there and in parts of Asia. For years it was absent from US sunscreens because it was not in the FDA's monograph; Wikipedia reports an FDA announcement of approval for sunscreens on 9 June 2026.
Human data include a series of 2020-2022 trials registered for a 6% bemotrizinol sunscreen, covering absorption, phototoxicity, photoallergy and irritation. No trial has studied it for appearance outcomes beyond sun protection.

name: Bisoctrizole

chain: Particle filter covers UVA and UVB
angle.text: Bisoctrizole (Tinosorb M) is a hybrid particulate filter in sunscreens abroad, sought by users wanting broad UVA and UVB coverage to protect skin from photoaging. Evidence is sunscreen-class and formulation-based; appearance outcomes of this filter alone are not studied.

summary: A particle-form UV filter (Tinosorb M) that covers UVA and UVB; common abroad, not US-approved.
note: Not an FDA-approved sunscreen active; Wikipedia flags some property claims as weakly sourced.
currentQuick:
Bisoctrizole is a sunscreen ingredient sold as microfine particles. It absorbs UVA and UVB and is sometimes described as a hybrid between chemical and mineral filters.
It is approved in the EU and several other regions, but not by the US FDA.
How it works: The particles absorb UV and dissipate it as heat. It is often used alongside other filters.
Risks and caveats: Sources describe minimal skin penetration and no estrogenic activity in lab tests. Environmental studies have measured it in sediment and tested aquatic species.
deepLead:
Bisoctrizole (INCI: methylene bis-benzotriazolyl tetramethylbutylphenol, MBBT; trade names Tinosorb M, Parsol Max) is a phenolic bis-benzotriazole UV absorber used in sunscreens. It is made as microfine particles, usually supplied as a roughly 50% aqueous suspension, and is described as a hybrid between organic and particulate filters.
It covers UVB and UVA and is reported to show little photodegradation. It is approved in the EU and other regions but has not been approved by the US FDA as a sunscreen active.
Research is mostly formulation, skin-penetration and environmental work. One small registered trial examined it alongside titanium dioxide in solar urticaria; no study has examined it as an appearance treatment.

name: Diethylamino hydroxybenzoyl hexyl benzoate

angle.text: DHHB (Uvinul A Plus) is a photostable UVA filter common in non-US sunscreens, valued by skincare users for protection against the UVA rays tied to wrinkles and dark spots. Support is lab and regulatory data, not trials of appearance.

summary: A photostable UVA sunscreen filter common outside the US; evidence is lab-based and regulatory.
note: Not a US sunscreen active; EU advisers set limits on a phthalate contaminant.
currentQuick:
DHHB is an oil-soluble sunscreen ingredient that absorbs UVA light. It is photostable and used in products in the EU, Japan and other markets.
It is not a US-approved sunscreen active, and no clinical trials of it alone were found.
How it works: It absorbs UVA near 354 nm and dissipates the energy, and studies show it interacts with other filters to help stabilise them.
Risks and caveats: The main regulatory concern is a manufacturing contaminant, di-n-hexyl phthalate, for which EU advisers recommended strict limits. Environmental monitoring studies have detected UV filters on beaches.
deepLead:
Diethylamino hydroxybenzoyl hexyl benzoate (DHHB), sold as Uvinul A Plus (BASF) and Parsol DHHB (DSM), is an oil-soluble organic UVA filter with an absorption maximum near 354 nm, noted for photostability and compatibility with other UV absorbers.
The EU approved it for sunscreens in 2005 at up to 10%, and it is also approved in several other markets including Japan; in the US, Wikipedia says it may be used for product protection rather than as a sunscreen active.
Published work on DHHB specifically is mostly laboratory-based: filter-filter photochemistry, formulation, and beach environmental monitoring. A notable regulatory discussion concerns a manufacturing contaminant, di-n-hexyl phthalate. No clinical trial of DHHB alone was found.

name: Ethylhexyl triazone

angle.text: Ethylhexyl triazone is a highly photostable UVB filter used in high-SPF sunscreens abroad, so people can reach strong protection that preserves skin tone and youthfulness. No clinical trials of it alone exist; the link to appearance comes from sunscreen use generally.

summary: A highly photostable UVB filter used in high-SPF products abroad; no clinical trials of it alone.
note: Not an approved US sunscreen active, per Grokipedia.
currentQuick:
Ethylhexyl triazone is an oil-soluble sunscreen ingredient that absorbs UVB light. It is used in products in the EU and elsewhere to help reach high SPF values.
Sources are thin: no clinical trials of it alone were found.
How it works: It absorbs UVB near 314 nm and dissipates the energy as heat; it is typically combined with UVA filters.
Risks and caveats: Sunscreen filters as a class are recognised photoallergens in dermatology clinics. Environmental studies have measured similar filters in wastewater, sludge and sediment.
deepLead:
Ethylhexyl triazone (octyl triazone, EHT; Uvinul T 150 from BASF, Parsol EHT from DSM-Firmenich) is an oil-soluble organic UVB filter with an absorption maximum near 314 nm. Its structure is a triazine ring bearing three 2-ethylhexyl benzoate groups.
Grokipedia describes it as highly photostable and used at low concentrations to raise SPF, and says it is permitted in the EU at up to 5% but lacks US approval as a sunscreen active. Its Wikipedia article is a short stub with no history or safety data.
Published research on EHT is mostly analytical, environmental and formulation work. No clinical trial of ethylhexyl triazone alone was found.
